verdicts.why: A's mark is a solid trunk with a felling notch and flared root base. It is one heavy, gapless silhouette that stays the same shape at 16 px and will cut, stamp and embroider cleanly, and the condensed IRONWOOD over tracked TREE CARE makes a deliberate, balanced lockup. B's concentric growth rings with a split relate to the subject but read as a generic target, the narrow white gaps go grey at 16 px and are risky for embroidery, and the name is set in a default-looking bold sans. A's silhouette could be misread as a boot, which is why the margin is only slight.

Both spell the name exactly and add nothing. B's mark is a solid stump with a notch cut into it, and it keeps the same clear silhouette at 32 and 16 px; it would also cut cleanly in one-color vinyl and embroider well. A's tree-ring mark turns into a muddy bullseye at 16 px, its thin white gaps are risky in embroidery, and the rings read as a target or a record. A's lockup is also a plain bold grotesk set in one line, while B's stacked condensed lockup feels more deliberate, though B's stump with its flared base can read a little like a boot.

A's mark falls apart in one ink and reversed: the BR letters disappear and leave a plain solid rounded square. That is fatal for a logo stamped in one ink on kraft bags and embroidered on aprons. B's chunky block 'B' holds the same shape at 16 px, in one color and reversed, and has no thin strokes, so it will stamp and embroider cleanly. Neither mark draws much on the mill or Blackwater subject, and A's BR in a rounded square is a generic app-icon monogram. B's serif wordmark is set more deliberately, so B wins on survival and craft.

B fails in one ink: its one-color and reversed marks turn into blank rounded squares and the BR monogram disappears, which is fatal for a logo stamped on kraft bags in one ink. 'BR' is also an odd set of initials for 'Blackwater Roasting Co.'. A's blocky B mark is crude and has little to do with the client's mill or Blackwater Falls, but it keeps the same solid shape at 16 px, in one ink and reversed, and it is paired with a well-set serif wordmark.

B makes nothing up. Its imagery rules are concrete enough to judge a photo against: the brewhouse in daylight, the bank building, families and dogs shown only with their permission, and cans on county shelves. Its voice examples also take in the bars and liquor stores that sell the cans. A has a richer palette and a useful contrast table that includes the failing pairs, but it adds a version year and a designated-driver promise the brief doesn't support. Its logo misuse list has no 'Don't' heading, so 'Stretch, skew, or rotate' reads as an instruction. B's one flaw is a swatch mismatch: the 'Foam on Green' tile shows dark text on foam. Its palette is also mostly muted neutrals, but the page is more complete and its layout is stronger.

verdicts.why: A sticks strictly to the brief and is fully usable: every color has a hex value, a named role and a contrast check, the type pairing and sizes are named, and the voice and imagery rules are specific to this client (the 7-barrel brewhouse, the old bank building, cans on county shelves). B has the richer, more brewery-specific palette and smart extras like the under-21 imagery rule and the TTB labeling note. But it adds details the brief doesn't support (a stone facade, a designated-driver promise, a 2026 version date), and its logo misuse list has no 'Don't' heading, so 'Stretch, skew, or rotate' reads as an instruction. A's palette is more muted and generic, and the lower page has some empty space, which keeps the margin slight.

verdicts.why: Neither page invents any facts. A's system fits this client better: a warm coral accent stands out from the usual teal and gray of dental brands, and every color has a clear role, including a rule that coral is not for text. A's three voice principles each come with a paired do and don't example written for nervous adults and toddlers, which a writer could actually follow. B gets credit for showing the logo in use and for a clear type scale, but its palette is generic and repeats the same white (#ffffff) as two separate colors, its contrast labels contradict each other (9.54:1 is marked both 'passes body' and 'passes large'), and it leaves a large empty area in the lower right.

B's system fits this client better. A warm coral accent against teal and a cream paper background sets it apart from the cold all-teal look that A shares with most dental brands. B's three voice principles each come with Do and Don't lines written for nervous adults and toddlers, so a writer could actually follow them. A is clean and factual, but its palette is nearly all one color and has two redundant pure-white swatches. Its contrast table also has small inconsistencies (13.1 vs 13.05, and a 9.54:1 pair marked only 'passes large'), and the white-on-teal logo version is printed too small to judge.

none: Implied office policy that patients 'can stop us at any time' and that each step is explained before it starts (example copy, not in the brief)

verdicts.why: A makes up three street names for the stops between the bus and Maya's stop (Elm St. & Birch Ln., Hollis Ct., Walnut Ave.). Those are facts the brief never gave, and a parent could act on them. B uses only the brief's facts: 3 stops, about 6 minutes, Mr. Dorsey, Oak St. and Ridgeway Ave. Its offline state clearly says the data is 2 minutes old, explains what will happen, and offers a large Try again button. A is more polished, with a better route timeline and status chips, but its 'Bus was away' wording is awkward. B's generic 'Stop' labels and the Refresh button on the live screen look a little like a wireframe, but that matters less than A's invented facts.

B makes up three street names that aren't in the brief (Elm St. & Birch Ln., Hollis Ct., Walnut Ave.), which is a serious fault on facts. A uses only the brief's content: Maya, bus 14, morning route, Oak St. and Ridgeway Ave., 3 stops, about 6 minutes, Mr. Dorsey. A's offline screen also keeps the parent's place, explains clearly that the data is from 2 minutes ago, and offers a large 'Try again' button. B has more polish, with iOS-style status icons and a dimmed last-known state, but its offline footer runs into the route card, and its invented stops outweigh the craft advantage.

verdicts.why: Both spell the name exactly and invent nothing. B's solid pixel-block mark holds up best at 16 px and in vinyl, but it reads as a mushroom or cross rather than a tree, the pixel-art style is wrong for an arborist, and the lockup is a default bold sans with a tiny mark, so craft and idea are weak. A's shield with a branch is still recognizable at 32 and 16 px and works in one ink and reversed, with a more deliberate serif lockup; its inner outline is thin and risky for embroidery and the hard-hat sticker, which is why A only wins slightly.

A survives at small sizes better: its blocky pixel tree is the same solid shape at 16 px. But it is a generic tree, which is close to what the client ruled out, it's drawn like a video-game sprite, and it's set in a default bold sans, so it fails on idea and craft. B's shield with a branch is deliberately drawn, with a balanced serif and small-caps lockup, and it holds up in one color and reversed. However, its thin inner outline and branch turn to mush at 16 px and would be risky as an embroidered or small sticker version, so B wins only narrowly. Neither invents any wording.

Both spell the name exactly and invent nothing. B's solid knocked-out mark keeps the same silhouette at 32 and 16 px and holds up in one ink and reversed. A's thin-line B with its tiny wave and peak detail turns to grey mush at 16 px and would be hard to embroider or stamp. A's idea (water and mountains inside the B) is more tied to Blackwater and its lockup is more refined, but B's mark is the one that works at every size the client needs, even though its broken B and building-like shape could read as a floppy disk.

A's mark is a solid gabled feed-mill shape with the B cut out of it, so it holds as the same shape at 32 and 16 px and works well for stamping, embroidery and reversing. B's outline B with a small wave or peak detail turns to grey mush at 16 px, and its thin strokes, hairline rule and small tracked 'ROASTING CO.' would fill in or vanish on kraft stamps and aprons. A's mill silhouette also comes from the client's own building, while B's water squiggle is more generic. A's wordmark is a plain default-looking serif, though, so A's craft is only adequate.
